newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin gives one more chance to his old aide.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin gives one more chance to his old aide.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin named Sergei Stepashin as his new justice minister on Wednesday, giving a rare second chance to a former security service chief disgraced during a bloody hostage drama two years ago.
Stepashin, 45, whose shy smile disguises a tough and ambitious character, paid with his job along with many other officials for Russia's humiliation during its war in Chechnya.

Yeltsin sacked him and interior minister Viktor Yerin after a group of pro-independence Chechen guerrillas led by field commander Shamil Basayev raided the southern Russian town Budennovsk in June 1995 and seized more than 1,000 hostages. At least 120 people were killed during the raid.
Lieutenant-General Stepashin's dismissal was regarded in Moscow as punishment for the Budennovsk incident and for Russia's broader humilation in Chechnya.
He is widely seen as one of the top officials who played a crucial role in starting the ill-fated military campaign to subdue Chechnya's independence drive in December 1994.
Tens of thousands people died in fighting which devastated the region and exposed Russia to strong international criticism for human rights violations before a peace deal was reached in August 1996.
Basayev is now a deputy prime minister in a Chechen government which appears committed to its initial aim -- winning full independence from Russia.
Several months before the main Chechen operation started, Stepashin covertly sent Russian tanks and crews to help the pro-Moscow opposition in Chechnya.
Then, starting from September 1994, unidentified warplanes bombed the regional capital Grozny several times.
Pro-independence forces seized several Russian servicemen who took part in the pro-Moscow opposition's attack on Grozny in November 1994.
This prompted a row in Moscow over the "freelance" use of army officers in FSB security service operations. But Stepashin kept his job.
Stepashin joined the Interior Ministry troops in 1973 as "politrabotnik" -- a member of the Communist Party watchdog corps in Soviet power structures.
He later switched to lecturing in a military academy and earned a doctorate for his work -- "The party leadership over fire brigades in Leningrad during World War Two".
During cautious perestroika politial reforms started by then-Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, the young officer stood for parliament, where he joined the liberal camp.
He spent some time in Supreme Soviet as the head of its security committee before finally establishing himself in the security ministry, which changed names several times during his stay.

Stepashin was one of the few security ministry officials left in place after an abortive hardline coup against Yeltsin in October 1993. In March 1994 he became the head of the newly formed Federal Security Service (FSB).
After his sacking, Stepashin kept a low profile working as the head of a relatively obscure administrative department of the government.
Sergei Vladimirovich Stepashin was born in the then Soviet military base of Port Arthur in China on March 2, 1952. He is married and has a son.
